claim: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) protect certain cold-adapted organisms from freezing to death by selectively adsorbing to internal ice crystals and inhibiting ice propagation.
source: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) protect certain cold-adapted organisms from freezing to death by selectively adsorbing to internal ice crystals and inhibiting ice propagation.
evidence: This is a general statement about AFP function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The molecular details of AFP adsorption-inhibition is uncertain but is proposed to involve the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
source: The molecular details of AFP adsorption-inhibition is uncertain but is proposed to involve the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
evidence: This statement acknowledges uncertainty while referencing an established theoretical framework.

claim: The spruce budworm Choristoneura fumiferana AFP binds indirectly to the prism ice face through a linear array of ordered water molecules that are structurally distinct from the ice.
source: The protein binds indirectly to the prism ice face through a linear array of ordered water molecules that are structurally distinct from the ice.
evidence: This claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutation of the ice binding surface disrupts water-ordering and abolishes activity.
source: Mutation of the ice binding surface disrupts water-ordering and abolishes activity.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data of mutant AFP presented in the manuscript.

claim: The adsorption of sbwAFP to ice is virtually irreversible.
source: The adsorption is virtually irreversible, and we confirm the ice growth inhibition is consistent with the Gibbs–Thomson law.
evidence: This is supported by simulation observations showing the AFP never detaching once bound.

claim: The ice growth inhibition by sbwAFP is consistent with the Gibbs–Thomson law.
source: The adsorption is virtually irreversible, and we confirm the ice growth inhibition is consistent with the Gibbs–Thomson law.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data showing agreement between theoretical and observed ice curvature.

claim: AFPs lower the freezing point and raise the melting point of ice through the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
source: By binding to ice, AFPs are thought to both lower the freezing point and raise the melting point of ice through the Gibbs–Thomson effect whereby adsorbed AFPs cause increased micro-curvature of the ice front (Yeh and Feeney, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The thermal hysteresis gap (TH) can range from a few tenths to over 6° depending on the specific AFP.
source: The resulting difference between the melting and freezing points, known as the thermal hysteresis gap (TH), can range from a few tenths to over 6°, depending on the specific AFP (Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Regular hexagonal ice (Ih) has three equivalent a-axes (a1–a3) which are parallel to three respective prism planes and perpendicular to the c-axis.
source: Regular hexagonal ice (Ih) has three equivalent a-axes (a1–a3) which are parallel to three respective prism planes and perpendicular to the c-axis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ice crystal structure.

claim: AFPs have evolved independently numerous times to bind stereo-selectively to ice in various orientations.
source: Remarkably AFPs have evolved independently numerous times to bind stereo-selectively to ice in various orientations, resulting in a structurally diverse protein family (Hew et al., 1985; Ko et al., 2003; Pentelute et al., 2008; Hakim et al., 2013; Middleton et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Polar fish do not normally experience temperatures much lower than the freezing point of sea water (−1.9°C).
source: Polar fish, for example, do not normally experience temperatures much lower than the freezing point of sea water (−1.9°C), and have AFPs that provide protection to just a few tenths of a degree below this.
evidence: This is established knowledge about polar fish environmental conditions.

claim: Fish AFPs often bind oblique to ice prism planes, typically forming hexagonal bipyramid crystals at temperatures within the TH gap.
source: Fish AFPs often bind oblique to ice prism planes, typically forming hexagonal bipyramid crystals at temperatures within the TH gap which rapidly grow as elongated spicules along the c-axis below the TH gap (Davies and Hew, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Insects are exposed to much lower terrestrial temperatures, often below −30°C.
source: In contrast insects which are exposed to much lower terrestrial temperatures, (often below −30°C), require AFPs with higher activity, possibly by selecting more effective prism and basal plane binding (Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect environmental conditions.

claim: Insects require AFPs with higher activity, possibly by selecting more effective prism and basal plane binding.
source: In contrast insects which are exposed to much lower terrestrial temperatures, (often below −30°C), require AFPs with higher activity, possibly by selecting more effective prism and basal plane binding (Lin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and involves speculation about mechanism.

claim: Slowly freezing solutions of dilute AFP will incorporate AFPs into the growing ice phase at roughly their original concentration, while non-AFPs and solutes are largely excluded.
source: Slowly freezing solutions of dilute AFP will incorporate AFPs into the growing ice phase at roughly their original concentration, while non-AFPs and solutes are largely excluded (Marshall et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Many structural studies have shown a correlation between the periodicity of the ice-binding surface elements of AFPs and their respective ice-binding planes.
source: Many structural studies have shown a correlation between the periodicity of the ice-binding surface elements of AFPs and their respective ice-binding planes, though it has not been entirely clear whether AFPs bind directly to ice or through some ordered water intermediate (Sharp, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It has not been entirely clear whether AFPs bind directly to ice or through some ordered water intermediate.
source: Many structural studies have shown a correlation between the periodicity of the ice-binding surface elements of AFPs and their respective ice-binding planes, though it has not been entirely clear whether AFPs bind directly to ice or through some ordered water intermediate (Sharp, 2011).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty in the field based on cited work.

claim: The TIP4P water model was used for simulations due to its ability to give realistic phase transformation behavior and superior freezing characteristics compared with the default TIP3P model.
source: The TIP4P water model (Jorgensen et al., 1983) was used for simulations due to its ability to give realistic phase transformation behavior and superior freezing characteristics compared with the default TIP3P model, its support by the NAMD software (Phillips et al., 2005), and its compatibility with biological CHARMM parameters (Glass et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: The melting point (Tm) of the TIP4P water model is 230.5 K.
source: Although the melting point (Tm) of the TIP4P water model is known to be 230.5 K, (García Fernández et al., 2006) it is highly unlikely such a water model will spontaneously freeze or remain frozen in simulation, particularly in the few degrees temperature range below Tm where AFPs exhibit their biological activity, due to the equilibrium radius R of the critical ice nucleus governed by the Gibbs–Thomson effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ice/water system employed consisted of 17,434 water molecules in a 51.5 × 126.6 × 83.9 Å box with periodic boundary conditions.
source: The ice/water system employed here consisted of 17,434 water molecules in a 51.5 × 126.6 × 83.9 Å box with PBCs, of which 1692 water molecules were harmonically constrained to an ideal prism ice lattice.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation system setup.

claim: 1692 water molecules were harmonically constrained to an ideal prism ice lattice to serve as the seed crystal.
source: The ice/water system employed here consisted of 17,434 water molecules in a 51.5 × 126.6 × 83.9 Å box with PBCs, of which 1692 water molecules were harmonically constrained to an ideal prism ice lattice. This served as the seed crystal while an additional 1049 water molecules below the seed were constrained in a 5 Å thick disordered layer to act as an ice barrier preventing downward ice growth, leaving a small wedge of mobile water between constrained layers as shown in Figure 3.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation system setup with reference to a figure.

claim: The seed ice crystal was angled approximately 4.3° with respect to the long axis to provide a continual ice growth mechanism.
source: The seed ice crystal included an additional small prism step to initiate step layer growth and the entire seed was angled such that the primary prism face was approximately 4.3° with respect to the long axis. The angle of the seed is such that step layer growth across the prism face reappears, due to PBCs, one layer higher to where it started, thus providing a continual ice growth mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the simulation system design.

claim: 32 independent, unconstrained simulations of at least 150 nanoseconds to as long as 250 ns duration were carried out at 228 K.
source: To characterize the binding mode of sbwAFP, 32 independent, unconstrained (apart from the waters constrained in the ice seed and ice-barrier) simulations of at least 150 nanoseconds (ns) to as long as 250 ns duration were carried out at 228 K.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol used.

claim: Definitive ice binding was observed 26 times with each binding event occurring with equivalent orientation with respect to the ice lattice.
source: Definitive ice binding was observed 26 times with each binding event occurring with equivalent orientation with respect to the ice lattice, though adsorbing at a number of different step heights.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations performed.

claim: Each of the definitive ice binding events incorporated a linear array of 6 water molecules bridging between the prism face and a row of conserved threonine residues.
source: Each of the definitive ice binding events incorporated a linear array of 6 water molecules bridging between the prism face and a row of conserved threonine residues (Thr 7, 23, 39, 54, 69, 84 and 101) as shown in Figure 4.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations with reference to a figure.

claim: The sbwAFP-bound water molecules were spaced approximately 4.5 Å apart, matching the periodicity of the prism face.
source: These water molecules had the same periodicity of the prism face, spaced approximately 4.5 Å apart.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data.

claim: The sbwAFP-bound water molecules were distinct from the bulk ice crystal, bridging between two prism face water molecules parallel along the c-axis which would normally be bridged by two water molecules in regular ice.
source: Interestingly they were distinct from the bulk ice crystal, bridging between two prism face water molecules parallel along the c-axis which would normally be bridged by two water molecules in regular ice as shown in Figure 5.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data with reference to a figure.

claim: The sbwAFP-bound water molecules had fully satisfied tetrahedral hydrogen bonding arrangements with two hydrogen bonds to the prism face ice water molecules and two hydrogen bonds to the hydroxyl groups of adjacent threonine residues.
source: The sbwAFP-bound water molecules had fully satisfied tetrahedral hydrogen bonding arrangements; two hydrogen bonds to the prism face ice water molecules and two hydrogen bonds to the hydroxyl groups of adjacent threonine residues of the sbwAFP ice binding face.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation data.

claim: 16 independent simulations of a sbwAFP mutant with 4 Thr to Leu substitutions at positions 7, 21, 39, 69 were performed, each of 250 ns length.
source: To further investigate the function of the ordered waters of the ice binding surface 16 independent simulations of a sbwAFP mutant (with 4 Thr to Leu substitutions at positions 7, 21, 39, 69) known to disrupt activity (Graether et al., 2000), were performed, each of 250 ns length.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol for mutant studies.

claim: No ice binding events were observed with the mutant sbwAFP, with all mutant AFPs diffusing ahead of the growing ice surface.
source: No ice binding events were observed with all mutant AFPs diffusing ahead of the growing ice surface in distinct contrast to the wild type protein.
evidence: This is a result from the mutant simulations.

claim: The Thr to Leu substitutions disrupt the binding of the ordered water to sbwAFP by removing the stabilizing hydroxyl side chain hydrogen bond interactions of the threonine residues.
source: The Thr to Leu substitutions disrupt the binding of the ordered water to sbwAFP by removing the stabilizing hydroxyl side chain hydrogen bond interactions of the threonine residues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural differences between threonine and leucine.

claim: Ordered waters are crucial in initiating sbwAFP recognition and binding to ice.
source: These results indicate ordered waters are crucial in initiating sbwAFP recognition and binding to ice and are suggestive of longer range protein-water interactions consistent with recent experimental findings by Meinster et al, of a similar beetle AFP from Dendroides canadensis, measured with terahertz spectroscopy (Meister et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation data and supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Three contiguous ∼1 μs MD simulations of sbwAFP adsorbed to an active ice front at temperatures of 225 K, 230 K and 232 K were run.
source: Three contiguous ∼1 μs MD simulations of sbwAFP adsorbed to an active ice front at temperatures of 225 K, 230 K and 232 K were run to test and simulate the adsorption-inhibition mechanism by observing subsequent ice growth as shown in Figure 7.
evidence: This describes the simulation protocol for testing adsorption-inhibition.

claim: At 225 K, the sbwAFP adsorbed to the ice front within 40 ns and within 150 ns the ice front displayed marked convex curvature creating cylindrical ice fronts.
source: In the first simulation the sbwAFP adsorbed from the solvent phase to the advancing ice front at 225 K (5 K below the model system Tm). The sbwAFP adsorbed to the ice front within 40 ns and within 150 ns the ice front displayed marked convex curvature creating cylindrical ice fronts as shown in Figure 8.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation at 225 K.

claim: By 250 ns at 225 K, the ice front had reached equilibrium with an averaged cylindrical radius of approximately 50 Å.
source: By 250 ns the ice front had reached equilibrium with an averaged cylindrical radius of approximately 50 Å.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation at 225 K.

claim: The ice fraction at 225 K equilibrated at 0.46 ± 0.01 (SD) measured over the 280 to 1000 ns time frame.
source: The ice fraction (defined as a proportion of total ice-like water molecules above the ice seed crystal), was measured over the 280 to 1000 ns time frame and found to equilibrate at 0.46 ± 0.01 (SD).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation at 225 K.

claim: AFP-free simulations froze almost completely within 150 ns.
source: In contrast AFP-free simulations froze almost completely within 150 ns.
evidence: This is a control simulation result.

claim: There is good qualitative agreement between theoretical Gibbs–Thomson curvature and the averaged ice front at 225 K.
source: The vacillating nature of the ice front in simulation makes quantitative measurement of the curvature difficult, however we find good qualitative agreement between theoretical Gibbs–Thomson curvature and the averaged ice front as shown in Figure 8 where the theoretical radius is overlaid on to the averaged simulation ice cross-section.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and theoretical predictions.

claim: When the temperature was raised to 230 K, the simulation showed a significant reduction of the ice fraction to an equilibrated value of 0.21 ± 0.02, calculated over the 1100 to 2130 ns time frame.
source: When the temperature was raised to 230 K, (the approximate system melting point Tm) the simulation showed a significant reduction of the ice fraction to an equilibrated value of 0.21 ± 0.02, (calculated over the 1100 to 2130 ns time frame) shown in Figure 8B.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation at 230 K.

claim: At 230 K, the sbwAFP remained bound to ice, stabilizing an ice protrusion directly beneath the AFP approximately 7 Å high relative to the main ice front.
source: The sbwAFP remained bound to ice, stabilizing an ice protrusion directly beneath the AFP approximately 7 Å high relative to the main ice front.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation at 230 K.

claim: At 232 K, the ice fraction equilibrated to an average of 0.15 ± 0.01 calculated over 2190 to 3160 ns time frame.
source: In the final contiguous simulation the temperature was raised to 232 K, (approximately 2 K above the simulation melting point) and showed further reduction in the ice fraction which equilibrated to an average of 0.15 ± 0.01 (calculated over 2190 to 3160 ns time frame).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the simulation at 232 K.

claim: At 232 K, the sbwAFP remained attached to an ice protrusion approximately 8.5 Å above the main ice plane which developed slight concave curvature with respect to the adsorbed protein.
source: The sbwAFP remained attached to the ice protrusion approximately 8.5 Å above the main ice plane which developed slight concave curvature with respect to the adsorbed protein (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation at 232 K.

claim: A continuation of the simulation at 235 K resulted in the detachment of the sbwAFP from the ice surface within 10 ns allowing further melting of the ice to a residual fraction of 0.08 ± 0.01.
source: A continuation of the simulation at 235 K resulted in the detachment of the sbwAFP from the ice surface within 10 ns allowing further melting of the ice to a residual fraction of 0.08 ± 0.01.
evidence: This is a result from the simulation at 235 K.

claim: The simulations demonstrate the Gibbs–Thomson effect showing how adsorbed protein induces ice-surface curvature and consequent melting and freezing inhibition of ice.
source: These simulations clearly demonstrate the Gibbs–Thomson effect showing how adsorbed protein induces ice-surface curvature and subsequent melting and freezing inhibition of ice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Previous estimations of the binding energy of AFPs to ice have varied greatly in the literature.
source: Previous estimations of the binding energy of AFPs to ice have varied greatly in the literature. Initial calculations from Cheng and Merz (1997) put the wfAFP binding energy of −157 kcal/mol while Dalal and Sönnichsen (2000) put the figure at −67 kcal/mol. Later estimates by Jorov et al. (2004) and Wierzbicki et al. (2007) both put the figure for wfAFP much lower at below −5 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is a summary of previous literature with citations.

claim: Microfluidic experiments by Celik et al. show that ice growth remains inhibited despite the exchange of the solution surrounding AFP-inhibited ice crystals with AFP-free buffer, suggesting there is little or no exchange of AFPs from the ice surface once bound.
source: Microfluidic experiments by Celik et al. (2013) show that ice growth remains inhibited despite the exchange of the solution surrounding AFP-inhibited ice crystals with AFP-free buffer, suggesting there is little or no exchange of AFPs from the ice surface once bound.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Antarctic notethenoid fishes internally accumulated ice does not melt as expected over summer warming periods.
source: This finding is further strengthened by recent field observations of Cziko et al. where it was found Antarctic notethenoid fishes internally accumulated ice does not melt as expected over summer warming periods (Cziko et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to field observations.

claim: The sbwAFP never detached once bound to ice, apart from deliberate melting events, even over the course of the extended millisecond range simulations at above melting temperatures.
source: Our own observations in this study suggest relatively strong binding of a magnitude similar to that proposed by Dalal and Sönnichsen (2000), with the sbwAFP never detaching once bound to ice, (apart from deliberate melting events), even over the course of the extended millisecond range simulations at above melting temperatures.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations performed in this study.

claim: sbwAFP activity depends on binding and arranging water in a similar periodicity to ice which in turn bind to the prism face of ice.
source: Our simulations have shown that sbwAFP activity depends on binding and arranging water in a similar periodicity to ice which in turn bind to the prism face of ice, and that the ordered water plays a crucial role in determining ice plane specificity and integrating into the ice lattice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Ordered water plays a crucial role in determining ice plane specificity and integrating into the ice lattice.
source: Our simulations have shown that sbwAFP activity depends on binding and arranging water in a similar periodicity to ice which in turn bind to the prism face of ice, and that the ordered water plays a crucial role in determining ice plane specificity and integrating into the ice lattice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Nutt and Smith's molecular dynamics simulations of sbwAFP in solution indicated water was more ice-like on its binding face at low temperatures and speculated that this preconfigured water was important for initial recognition and binding events.
source: This conclusion is supported by previous work by Nutt and Smith (2008) whose molecular dynamics simulations of sbwAFP in solution indicated water was more ice-like on its binding face at low temperatures and speculated that this preconfigured water was important for initial recognition and binding events.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous computational work.

claim: Recent work by Midya and Bandyopadhyay simulating insect AFP from Tenebrio molitor found equivalent arrangements of bound water molecules emphasizing the importance of the hydroxyl groups of the ice-binding threonine residues.
source: Recent work by Midya and Bandyopadhyay (2014) simulating insect AFP from Tenebrio molitor with a similar ice binding surface to sbwAFP in water have also found equivalent arrangements of bound water molecules emphasizing the importance of the hydroxyl groups of the ice-binding threonine residues.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent computational work.

claim: The putative ice-binding threonine residues of the alpha helical wfAFP can be substituted to structurally similar but hydrophobic valine residue with little effect on activity.
source: Contrary to this, as mentioned previously, it is noteworthy that the putative ice-binding threonine residues of the alpha helical wfAFP can be substituted to structurally similar but hydrophobic valine residue with little effect on activity (Haymet et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: wfAFP ice binding does not depend on the threonine hydroxyl group.
source: This shows wfAFP ice binding does not depend on the threonine hydroxyl group, even suggesting a hydrophobic mode of interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental result.

claim: Many of the solved AFP crystal structures have been found to contain ordered waters which have been postulated to integrate directly into the ice lattice.
source: Many of the solved AFP crystal structures have been found to contain ordered waters which have been postulated to integrate directly into the ice lattice (Liou et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: In the recently determined structure for mpAFP, bound waters exhibited an extensive 'clathrate-like' network that matched ice lattice dimensions.
source: In a recently determined structure for a highly active bacterial AFP from Marinomonas primiryensis (mpAFP), bound waters exhibited an extensive 'clathrate-like' network that matched ice lattice dimensions (Garnham et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: mpAFP appears to bind to all ice plane orientations, rather than specific ones.
source: Interestingly, unlike most AFPs, mpAFP appears to bind to all ice plane orientations, rather than specific ones.
evidence: This is a statement about mpAFP properties based on established knowledge.

claim: mpAFP's binding to all ice plane orientations may result from extended ice-like ordering of water from the ice binding surfaces interacting with ice in non-specific orientations, perhaps in a process similar to ice sintering.
source: This may result from extended ice-like ordering of water from the ice binding surfaces interacting with ice in non-specific orientations, perhaps in a process similar to ice sintering (Kuroiwa, 1961).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation with citation to a related phenomenon.

claim: Previous AFP simulations have focused on modeling prearranged AFPs at the ice-water interface at equilibrium and have not yet tackled free AFP interacting with an actively growing ice interface.
source: As noted in a recent review by Nada and Furukawa (2012), previous AFP simulations have focused on modeling prearranged AFPs at the ice-water interface at equilibrium and have not yet tackled free AFP interacting with an actively growing ice interface which would reveal more mechanisms of the molecular process and be less biased to initial positioning.
evidence: This is a summary of the state of the field with citation.

claim: The freely diffusing MD simulations of AFP spontaneously adsorbing and inhibiting an active ice surface model have demonstrated that simulations can be used to provide detailed insight into molecular processes like crystal inhibition and modification.
source: Our freely diffusing MD simulations of AFP spontaneously adsorbing and inhibiting an active ice surface model have demonstrated that simulations can be used to provide detailed insight into molecular processes like crystal inhibition and modification.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the simulation approach.

claim: The simulations presented demonstrate key aspects of the AFP mechanisms: the process of molecular surface recognition and irreversible adsorption inhibition of the ice surface.
source: We have presented simulations of the sbwAFP spontaneously interacting with a growing ice surface and demonstrated key aspects of the AFP mechanisms; namely the process of molecular surface recognition and irreversible adsorption inhibition of the ice surface.
evidence: This is a summary of the key findings from the simulations.

claim: The Gibbs–Thomson formula agrees closely with the simulated inhibition of the growing ice front.
source: We have shown that the Gibbs–Thomson formula agrees closely with the simulated inhibition of the growing ice front, and demonstrated irreversibility of binding by free energy analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing simulation results with theoretical predictions.

claim: This is one of the first computer simulations to provide a complete in silico demonstration of a protein's biological function.
source: This is one of the first computer simulations to provide a complete in silico demonstration of a protein's biological function.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the work in the context of computational biology.

claim: Molecular simulations were performed using NAMD2.9 with CHARM22 forcefield employing a TIP4P water model.
source: Molecular simulations were performed using NAMD2.9 (Wierzbicki et al., 1997) with CHARM22 (MacKerell et al., 1998) forcefield employing a TIP4P water model supported on both IBM BlueGene/P and BlueGene/Q architecture.
evidence: This is a description of the computational methods used.

claim: The sbwAFP model was based on the pdb structure 1M8N.
source: The sbwAFP model was based on the pdb structure 1M8N (Leinala et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the source of the protein structure used in simulations.

claim: Simulations were run with periodic boundary conditions using the NPT ensemble at various temperatures (225, 228, 230, 232 and 235 K) and 1 bar pressure employing Langevin dynamics.
source: Simulations were run with PBCs using the NPT ensemble at various temperatures (225, 228, 230, 232 and 235 K) and 1 bar pressure employing Langevin dynamics.
evidence: This describes the simulation conditions used.

claim: The sbwAFP has a β-helix structure with a triangular cross-section forming three parallel β-sheet faces and a hydrophobic core.
source: SbwAFP has a β-helix structure with a triangular cross-section forming three parallel β-sheet faces and a hydrophobic core as shown in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a description of the protein structure with reference to a figure.

claim: The ice binding face of sbwAFP has a regular array of repeating threonine-x-threonine (T-X-T) motifs whereby the spacing between threonine residues match the repeat spacing parallel to the c-axis of ice of approximately 7.4 Å.
source: The ice binding face has a regular array of repeating threonine-x-threonine (T-X-T) motifs whereby the spacing between threonine residues match the repeat spacing parallel to the c-axis of ice of approximately 7.4 Å and motifs on adjacent β-strands closely match the a-axis repeating dimensions of the prism face of ice of 4.5 Å.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of the ice binding surface.

claim: Motifs on adjacent β-strands of sbwAFP closely match the a-axis repeating dimensions of the prism face of ice of 4.5 Å.
source: The ice binding face has a regular array of repeating threonine-x-threonine (T-X-T) motifs whereby the spacing between threonine residues match the repeat spacing parallel to the c-axis of ice of approximately 7.4 Å and motifs on adjacent β-strands closely match the a-axis repeating dimensions of the prism face of ice of 4.5 Å.
evidence: This is a description of the structural features of the ice binding surface.

claim: The second row of threonine residues of the ice-binding surface is particularly sensitive to mutation, with replacement of the threonines drastically reducing sbwAFP's potency as an AFP.
source: The second row of threonine residues of the ice-binding surface is particularly sensitive to mutation, with replacement of the threonines drastically reducing sbwAFP's potency as an AFP (Graether et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: sbwAFP induces a non-colligative freezing point depression of ice by up to 6°C.
source: In addition to inducing a non-colligative freezing point depression of ice by up to 6°C, sbwAFP also demonstrates a significant melting inhibition (super-heating) of ice of up to 0.44°C (Celik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: sbwAFP demonstrates a significant melting inhibition (super-heating) of ice of up to 0.44°C.
source: In addition to inducing a non-colligative freezing point depression of ice by up to 6°C, sbwAFP also demonstrates a significant melting inhibition (super-heating) of ice of up to 0.44°C (Celik et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: For a single degree of supercooling, assuming spherical geometry, the critical radius of an ice embryo is about 518 Å containing approximately 18 million water molecules.
source: For example, assuming spherical geometry, for a single degree of supercooling the critical radius of an ice embryo is about 518 Å containing approximately 18 million water molecules, which is currently computationally prohibitive to model (see 'Materials and methods' for calculation).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the Gibbs-Thomson equation.

claim: Early computational simulations of winter-flounder AFP by Wen and Laursen, Jorgensen et al., and Madura et al. firmly established the correlation of the distance between regularly spaced polar threonine residues and that of water molecules of the ice lattice of the {2021} pyramidal ice plane in the [112] direction.
source: Early computational simulations of winter-flounder AFP (wfAFP) by Wen and Laursen (1992); Jorgensen et al. (1993); Madura et al. (1994) firmly established the correlation of the distance between regularly spaced polar threonine residues and that of water molecules of the ice lattice of the {2021} pyramidal ice plane in the [112] direction by searching for energetically stable conformations.
evidence: This is a summary of previous computational work with citations.

claim: Knight et al. showed the preferential binding orientation of wfAFP on single crystal ice hemisphere.
source: This was in agreement with previous experimental work of Knight et al which showed the preferential binding orientation of wfAFP on single crystal ice hemisphere (Knight et al., 1991) and also the later work of Sicheri and Yang who determined the wfAFP crystal structure (Sicheri and Yang, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to experimental work.

claim: Sicheri and Yang determined the wfAFP crystal structure.
source: This was in agreement with previous experimental work of Knight et al which showed the preferential binding orientation of wfAFP on single crystal ice hemisphere (Knight et al., 1991) and also the later work of Sicheri and Yang who determined the wfAFP crystal structure (Sicheri and Yang, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to structural work.

claim: Cheng and Merz used molecular dynamics simulations of solvated wfAFP in the bound conformation to the {2021} pyramidal plane to propose key hydrogen bond interactions between polar residues and the ice surface, suggesting that hydrogen bonds were the primary driving force of ice adsorption.
source: Cheng and Merz further expanded this work using molecular dynamics simulations of solvated wfAFP in the bound conformation to the {2021} pyramidal plane to propose key hydrogen bond interactions between polar residues and the ice surface, suggesting that hydrogen bonds were the primary driving force of ice adsorption (Cheng and Merz, 1997).
evidence: This is a summary of previous computational work with citation.

claim: Mutational work by the groups of Harding and Laursen raised questions about the nature of the wfAFP-ice interaction; conservative substitution of threonine residues for serine abolished activity, while threonine to valine substitution retained AFP activity.
source: However, this model was to be short lived as mutational work by the groups of Harding and Laursen (Zhang and Laursen, 1998; Haymet et al., 1999) raised questions about the nature of the wfAFP-ice interaction; conservative substitution of threonine residues for serine abolished activity, while threonine to valine substitution, which removed the proposed threonine hydroxyl–ice interactions surprisingly retained AFP activity.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental mutational work with citations.

claim: Dalal and Sönnichsen and Jorov et al. employed Monte Carlo simulations of the wfAFP on the pyramidal plane, both groups finding that hydrophobic interactions contributed significantly to the adsorption to ice.
source: Spurred by the paradoxical mutant wfAFP results both Dalal and Sönnichsen (2000) and Jorov et al. (2004) employed Monte Carlo simulations of the wfAFP on the pyramidal plane, both groups finding that hydrophobic interactions contributed significantly to the adsorption to ice.

claim: Wierzbicki et al. proposed that wfAFP doesn't bind directly to ice but rather accumulates at the ice-water interface with preference for the hydrophobic over the hydrophilic face facing the ice.
